lead: On the feast of St Mariam Thresia the four readings trace the road of a life given wholly to God. Abram hears “Go from your country” and goes, not knowing the way. Sirach warns the one who comes to serve the Lord to be ready for testing, for gold is tried in fire. Paul says the secret of such a life: “it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.” And in Matthew the King reveals where that life is lived: in the hungry, the stranger, the sick and the prisoner, “you did it to me.” Call, testing, union with Christ, and service of the least: that is the shape of every holy life, and it is the shape of the life of the saint of Puthenchira.

r.h: Go to the land that I will show you
set: After the story of Babel, where people tried to make a name for themselves (11:4), Genesis narrows to one family. Terah had set out from Ur of the Chaldeans with his son Abram, Sarai his wife and his grandson Lot, and settled at Haran in the north (11:31). There the Lord speaks to Abram. This is the turning point of Genesis: from the scattering of the nations the story moves to the man through whom all the nations will be blessed.
Sarai is barren (11:30), and Abram is seventy-five years old. Everything in the promise of a great nation is humanly impossible. That is the point: the future will be God’s gift.
str: v. 1: the command: go from country, kindred and father’s house, to a land God will show.
vv. 2–3: the promises: a great nation, blessing, a great name, a blessing to others, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
v. 4: the response: Abram went, as the Lord had told him.
kw: A doubled Hebrew form, literally “go for yourself”. The same rare form returns when God tells Abraham to go to the land of Moriah with Isaac (22:2). Abraham’s life with God begins and reaches its height with the same call to set out.
The word and its verb occur five times in verses 2–3. After the curses of Genesis 3–11, blessing begins again, and it is meant to spread: “you will be a blessing.”
Not only Israel. From the first call, God’s plan for Abram has all humanity in view.
vv: Now the Lord said to Abram, “Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you.
The three circles grow narrower and dearer: land, clan, family home. God does not name the land. Abram must go first and be shown later.
I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.
At Babel people wanted to make a name for themselves (11:4). Here God gives the name. Greatness is received, not seized.
and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
Paul reads this as the Gospel announced beforehand: the nations would be blessed through faith, in Abraham’s offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16).
So Abram went, as the Lord had told him; and Lot went with him.
No words from Abram, only obedience. His answer is his journey.
ch: The Catechism calls Abraham the model of the obedience of faith: “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to set out for a place that he was to receive as an inheritance” (Hebrews 11:8; CCC 144–145). It teaches that with Abraham God began to gather scattered humanity, and that the people descended from him would be the root onto which the Gentiles would be grafted (CCC 59–60). The Roman Canon names him “our father in faith”, and the Church honours him as father of all who believe (CCC 146).

r.h: Gold is tested in the fire
set: The Book of Sirach was written in Hebrew in Jerusalem about 180 BC by a teacher named Jesus son of Sirach, and translated into Greek in Egypt by his grandson after 132 BC, as the grandson tells in his prologue. It is one of the books the Catholic Church receives as Scripture (CCC 120) and was used so much in teaching new Christians that it was long called Ecclesiasticus, “the church book”.
Chapter 1 praised wisdom and the fear of the Lord. Chapter 2 turns to the cost: anyone who sets out to serve God must expect trials, and must cling to him in them.
str: v. 1: the warning: if you come to serve the Lord, prepare for testing.
vv. 2–3: set your heart right, be steadfast, cling to him.
v. 4: accept what comes, and be patient in humiliation.
v. 5: the image: gold in the fire, the acceptable in the furnace of humiliation.
v. 6: trust, walk straight, hope in him.
kw: The usual address of a wise teacher to his pupil (as in Proverbs). Testing is spoken of within a relationship of love, as a father speaks to a son.
The same Greek word as in the Lord’s Prayer, “do not bring us to the time of trial” (Matthew 6:13). Here it means the trials that prove and purify faith.
Being brought low: loss, shame, failure. Sirach says this low place can be a furnace where the soul is refined.
vv: My child, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing.
An honest beginning. God’s service is not a guarantee of an easy life; it is a guarantee of his company.
Cling to him and do not depart, so that your last days may be prosperous.
“Cling” is the word of a bond that holds, like the bond of husband and wife (Genesis 2:24 in Greek uses a related verb).
For gold is tested in the fire, and those found acceptable, in the furnace of humiliation.
The same image appears in Wisdom 3:6 and 1 Peter 1:7. Fire does not destroy gold; it makes it pure.
Trust in him, and he will help you; make your ways straight, and hope in him.
Three verbs, trust, walk straight, hope: the whole programme of the tested believer.
ch: The Church reads Sirach as a teacher of the moral life and of perseverance. The Catechism teaches that hope keeps us from discouragement and sustains us in times of abandonment (CCC 1818). The saints often spoke of trials as God’s refining fire. The image of gold in the furnace is taken up in the New Testament, where faith tested by fire is more precious than gold (1 Peter 1:7).

set: Paul has just told how he opposed Peter at Antioch when Peter withdrew from eating with Gentile believers (2:11–14). He goes on to state the heart of his Gospel: we are made righteous not by works of the Law but through faith in Jesus Christ (2:16). These three verses are his personal testimony, among the most intimate words he ever wrote.
str: v. 19a: through the Law I died to the Law, to live for God.
vv. 19b–20a: crucified with Christ; no longer I, but Christ living in me.
v. 20b: my life now is faith in the Son of God who loved me and gave himself for me.
v. 21: I do not set aside the grace of God; if righteousness came through the Law, Christ died for nothing.
kw: A Greek perfect tense: something done once that still stands. In baptism the believer is joined to the death of Christ (Romans 6:3–6), and lives from that moment on.
Not mere imitation of Christ from outside, but his life within. The “I” is not destroyed; it is healed and filled.
God’s gift, given without our deserving. To seek righteousness by our own efforts alone would be to treat the Cross as unnecessary.
vv: For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
The Law itself, by pointing to Christ and by showing sin, led Paul to die to it as a way of being made righteous. He does not despise the Law; he says it has done its work.
it is no longer I who live, but it is Christ who lives in me.
The great sentence of Christian mysticism. The saints have read it as the goal of every life of prayer: that Christ may live his life again in us.
I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
The Greek can also be read “by the faith of the Son of God”, that is, his faithfulness; the NRSV notes this. Either way the life rests on him. And Paul says “me”: the love of the Cross is personal.
ch: The Catechism quotes these words to teach that Jesus knew and loved each one of us during his life, his agony and his Passion, and gave himself up for each one: “The Son of God… loved me and gave himself for me” (CCC 478). It also teaches that justification is the work of God’s grace, received in faith and baptism, and that it does not exclude but brings forth our cooperation in love (CCC 1987–1993). St John Chrysostom, commenting on this verse, notes that Paul makes the love of Christ for all the world his own, as if Christ had died for him alone (in substance, Commentary on Galatians).

set: This is the last of Jesus’ teachings in Matthew before the Passion (26:1–2). After the parables of the bridesmaids and the talents, Jesus describes the judgment itself. The Son of Man comes as King and Shepherd, and all the nations are gathered before him.

In the land of Israel sheep and goats often grazed together in one flock and were separated at evening. The scene is homely and solemn at once. Today’s reading gives the blessed side of the judgment (25:31–40); the Gospel continues with those on the left (25:41–46).
str: vv. 31–33: the coming of the Son of Man in glory; all nations gathered; sheep and goats separated.
vv. 34–36: the King’s welcome: inherit the kingdom, for I was hungry, thirsty, a stranger, naked, sick, in prison.
vv. 37–39: the surprise of the righteous: when did we see you?
v. 40: the answer: just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.
kw: Jesus’ favourite title for himself, drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a human being” (literally “like a son of man”) receives everlasting dominion over all peoples.
The smallest, the lowest. Jesus calls them “members of my family”, literally “my brothers”. He takes the place of the person no one notices.
An inheritance is given because one is a child, not earned as wages. The kingdom “prepared for you from the foundation of the world” is the Father’s gift to his children.
vv: When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory.
The one who will judge is the one who was judged and crucified. The Judge is the Saviour.
for I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me,
Six needs, and none is unusual. Holiness here is made of ordinary acts of mercy.
Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when was it that we saw you hungry and gave you food
The righteous did not know they were serving Christ. Their love was simple and unself-conscious.
just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.
Christ identifies himself with the poor. Love of neighbour is not something next to love of Christ; in the least, it is love of Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus identifies himself with the poor of every kind and makes active love toward them the condition for entering his kingdom (CCC 544), and that the Eucharist commits us to the poor: to receive in truth the Body and Blood of Christ given up for us, we must recognise Christ in the poorest, his brethren (CCC 1397). It also reminds us that we will be judged on our love (CCC 1022, quoting St John of the Cross). St Teresa of Calcutta summed up her life’s work with this verse, counting its words on her fingers: “you did it to me.”

qa: Does Matthew 25 mean that only good works matter, and faith is not important?

No. The righteous are called “blessed by my Father”: their life comes from God’s grace. Faith in Christ and love for the least belong together, as root and fruit. By grace our works of love have real worth before God (CCC 2008–2011), and faith that does not act in love is not living faith (Galatians 5:6). Matthew 25 shows what living faith looks like.
Why is Sirach in the Catholic Bible but not in some other Bibles?

Sirach belongs to the books found in the Greek Old Testament used by the early Church. The Church accepted it as inspired from early times; the Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397), and later the Councils of Florence and Trent, list it among the sacred books (CCC 120). The Reformers placed it among the Apocrypha. Catholics and Orthodox read it as the word of God.

Mariam Thresia Chiramel Mankidiyan was born in 1876 at Puthenchira, in the present Thrissur district of Kerala. She gave her life to prayer, penance and the service of families, the sick and the dying, visiting homes and nursing those whom others avoided. In 1914 she founded the Congregation of the Holy Family. She died on 8 June 1926, was beatified by Pope St John Paul II in 2000 and canonised by Pope Francis on 13 October 2019.
rite: St Mariam Thresia is a daughter of our own Syro-Malabar Church. Like Abram she left the security she knew to follow a call that others did not understand; like the gold in Sirach she passed through long trials, both inner darkness and misunderstanding; and like Paul she longed for Christ to live in her. Her life is the Gospel of today lived out in Kerala villages: she went to the homes of the poor and the sick, cared for the dying, and saw the family as the place where Christ is served.

The Congregation of the Holy Family, which she founded, continues this work. On her feast, families can pray together for those in their parish who are sick, lonely or in need, and choose one act of the six named by the King to do this week, as a family.
study: Abram went without knowing where. What is God asking me to leave or begin, even before I see the whole road?
Sirach says gold is tested in fire. Looking back, how has a trial purified my faith?
Paul says, “it is Christ who lives in me.” In which part of my day do I most need to let Christ live and act instead of my own self?
St Mariam Thresia served Christ in families and the sick. Which of the six works in Matthew 25 can my family do together this week?
